title: Jira vs Plane
comparison_markdown:
# Jira vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Jira and Plane are two project management tools that help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is useful for teams currently using Jira who are considering switching to Plane, possibly due to cost or data ownership concerns. The core use case for both tools is issue tracking and project management, and someone would switch if they need more control over their data or a self-hosted solution.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Jira is a paid service, while Plane is free and open-source.
* Data ownership: Jira stores data on its servers, while Plane allows users to host their data on their own servers.
* Setup complexity: Jira has a more complex setup process, while Plane is relatively simple to set up.
* Scalability: Jira is designed for large teams and enterprises, while Plane is better suited for small to medium-sized teams.
* Integration with Git: Jira has native integration with Git, while Plane uses a third-party plugin for Git integration.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Jira | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.75-$14.50/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $387.50-$725.00/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,550.00-$2,900.00/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Jira:**
* Pros:
	+ Robust feature set
	+ Native integration with Git
	+ Large community of users and developers
	+ Good customer support
* Cons:
	+ Expensive, especially for large teams
	+ Data is stored on Jira's servers
	+ Complex setup process
**Plane:**
* Pros:
	+ Free and open-source
	+ Self-hosted option for data control
	+ Simple setup process
	+ Customizable
* Cons:
	+ Limited scalability
	+ Limited native integrations
	+ Requires technical expertise for self-hosting
	+ Limited customer support

## When to Choose Each
Jira is a good choice for large teams and enterprises that need a robust feature set and native integration with Git. It is also a good choice for teams that are already invested in the Atlassian ecosystem. Plane, on the other hand, is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that need a simple, self-hosted project management solution. It is also a good choice for teams that are looking for a free and open-source alternative to Jira.
Plane is suitable for teams that value data control and customization, and are willing to invest time in setting up and maintaining their own server.

## Migration Path
1. Export your data from Jira in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up a Plane server and create a new project.
3. Use the Plane import tool to import your data from the CSV or JSON file.
4. Configure your Plane project to match your Jira workflow.
5. Test your Plane project to ensure that everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Plane is not yet production-ready for most users, as it lacks some of the features and polish of Jira. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Plane's self-hosted option requires a significant amount of technical expertise to set up and maintain. However, for small to medium-sized teams that need a simple, self-hosted project management solution, Plane is a good choice. We recommend switching to Plane if you are a small team that values data control and customization, and are willing to invest time in setting up and maintaining your own server.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that need a simple project management solution and do not require native integration with Git.
* Teams that value data control and customization, and are willing to invest time in setting up and maintaining their own server.
* Teams that are looking for a free and open-source alternative to Jira.
* Teams that do not need a robust feature set and are willing to compromise on scalability.
* Teams that are already using other open-source tools and want to integrate Plane into their existing workflow.

## FAQ
### Is Plane free?
Yes, Plane is free and open-source. However, you will need to pay for your own server costs if you choose to self-host.
### Can I integrate Plane with Git?
Yes, Plane can be integrated with Git using a third-party plugin.
### Is Plane suitable for large teams?
No, Plane is not yet suitable for large teams due to its limited scalability.
### Can I import my data from Jira into Plane?
Yes, you can import your data from Jira into Plane using the Plane import tool.
### Is Plane production-ready?
Not yet, Plane is still in development and lacks some of the features and polish of Jira.

title: Trello vs WeKan
comparison_markdown:
# Trello vs WeKan

## Overview

Trello is a visual kanban board tool from Atlassian, simple and beginner-friendly. WeKan is an open-source kanban board offering the same card/list/board model without vendor dependency.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Trello paid plans start at $5/user/month; WeKan is completely free
- **Data control**: WeKan runs on your own server; Trello data lives on Atlassian infrastructure
- **Features**: Trello has a larger Power-Ups marketplace; WeKan covers core kanban features
- **Setup**: Trello requires zero setup; WeKan requires a server
- **Customization**: WeKan open-source code can be extended; Trello cannot

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Trello | WeKan |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $5+/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Trello

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### WeKan

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [wekan/wekan](https://github.com/wekan/wekan) * ~20k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Trello if:** Trello suits individuals and small teams wanting instant zero-setup kanban with integrations to Slack, Google Drive, and GitHub.

**Choose WeKan if:** WeKan is ideal for teams wanting full data ownership or air-gapped deployments.

## Migration Path

Export Trello boards as JSON, then use WeKan Trello importer in Settings to recreate boards, lists, and cards.

## Our Take

WeKan is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Trello tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your WeKan instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Trello, switching to self-hosted WeKan will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Trello until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Trello paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is WeKan free to use?
Yes. WeKan is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Trello to WeKan?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Trello data, follow the WeKan import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does WeKan get regular updates?
Yes. WeKan has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use WeKan without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if WeKan development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Trello](https://trello.com) and [WeKan](https://wekan.github.io) before making decisions.*

# Zoom vs Jitsi Meet (2026)

## Overview
Zoom and Jitsi Meet are video conferencing tools that enable teams to conduct virtual meetings and collaborate remotely. This comparison is beneficial for teams and individuals who are looking for a reliable and feature-rich video conferencing solution, and are considering switching from Zoom to Jitsi Meet due to concerns about data ownership and cost.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Zoom offers a free plan with limited features, while Jitsi Meet is completely free and open-source.
* Data Ownership: Jitsi Meet allows users to self-host their servers, giving them full control over their data, while Zoom stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup Complexity: Zoom has a more straightforward setup process, while Jitsi Meet requires more technical expertise to self-host.
* Scalability: Zoom has better scalability and can handle larger meetings, while Jitsi Meet can be more resource-intensive.
* Screen Sharing: Zoom has more advanced screen sharing features, including the ability to share multiple screens and annotate shared content, while Jitsi Meet has more limited screen sharing capabilities.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Zoom | Jitsi Meet |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $13.33+/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $13.33+/user/month = $666.50/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $13.33+/user/month = $2,666/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Zoom:**
* Easy to use and set up
* High-quality video and audio
* Advanced features like screen sharing and annotation
* Large user base and community support
* Integrates with many third-party tools
**Jitsi Meet:**
* Free and open-source
* Self-hosting option for full data control
* Customizable and extensible
* End-to-end encryption for secure meetings
* Limited user interface and features compared to Zoom

## When to Choose Each
Zoom is a good choice for large teams or enterprises that need advanced features and scalability, and are willing to pay for them. It is also a good option for users who are already familiar with the platform and have invested in its ecosystem. On the other hand, Jitsi Meet is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams or individuals who value data ownership and control, and are looking for a free and open-source solution. It is also a good option for users who are technically savvy and can self-host their own servers.
Jitsi Meet is suitable for teams that prioritize security and flexibility, and are willing to invest time in setting up and customizing their own servers. It is also a good choice for users who are looking for a solution that can be integrated with other open-source tools and platforms.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Zoom meeting data and settings in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up a Jitsi Meet server and configure it to your needs.
3. Import your meeting data and settings into Jitsi Meet using the import tool.
4. Test your Jitsi Meet setup and ensure that all features are working as expected.
5. Update your meeting links and invitations to point to your new Jitsi Meet server.

## Our Take
Jitsi Meet is not yet production-ready for most users, as it requires technical expertise to set up and configure. However, for users who value data ownership and control, it can be a good option. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Jitsi Meet can be resource-intensive and may require significant server resources to handle large meetings.
Jitsi Meet's self-hosting option provides full data control, but it also means that users are responsible for maintaining and updating their own servers. This can be a significant burden for non-technical users.
We recommend switching to Jitsi Meet if you are a small to medium-sized team or individual who values data ownership and control, and are willing to invest time in setting up and customizing your own server. However, if you are a large enterprise or require advanced features and scalability, Zoom may still be the better choice.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who do not need advanced features like screen sharing and annotation.
* Individuals who value data ownership and control, and are willing to self-host their own servers.
* Teams who are already using other open-source tools and platforms, and want to integrate Jitsi Meet into their existing ecosystem.
* Users who are looking for a free and open-source solution, and are willing to invest time in setting up and customizing their own servers.
* Developers who want to customize and extend Jitsi Meet to meet their specific needs.

## FAQ
### Is Jitsi Meet free?
Yes, Jitsi Meet is completely free and open-source.
### Can I self-host Jitsi Meet?
Yes, Jitsi Meet provides a self-hosting option, which gives you full control over your data and servers.
### Does Jitsi Meet have end-to-end encryption?
Yes, Jitsi Meet provides end-to-end encryption for secure meetings.
### Can I import my Zoom meeting data into Jitsi Meet?
Yes, Jitsi Meet provides an import tool that allows you to import your Zoom meeting data and settings.
### Is Jitsi Meet compatible with all browsers?
No, Jitsi Meet may not be compatible with all browsers, and may require specific browser versions or configurations to work properly.

# Airtable vs NocoDB (2026)

## Overview
Airtable and NocoDB are two popular database management tools used for organizing and tracking data. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and teams looking to switch from Airtable to NocoDB, particularly those seeking more control over their data and a self-hosted solution. The core use case for both tools is to provide a flexible and customizable database for various applications, with the key reason to switch being the desire for greater data ownership and scalability.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Airtable offers a free plan and paid plans starting at $10-$20 per user/month, while NocoDB is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: NocoDB allows for full data ownership since it is self-hosted, whereas Airtable stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Airtable has a more user-friendly interface and is generally easier to set up, while NocoDB requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: NocoDB is more scalable due to its self-hosted nature, allowing for greater control over resources and performance.
* Feature difference: Airtable has a more developed ecosystem of integrations and plugins, while NocoDB has a more open and customizable architecture.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Airtable | NocoDB |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $10-$20/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $500-$1000/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2000-$4000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Airtable:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Large ecosystem of integrations and plugins
* Scalable and performant
* Collaborative features
* Limited control over data ownership
**NocoDB:**
* Self-hosted and open-source
* Full control over data ownership
* Highly customizable and scalable
* Free and cost-effective
* Steeper learning curve and more technical expertise required

## When to Choose Each
Airtable is suitable for teams of all sizes that prioritize ease of use, a large ecosystem of integrations, and collaborative features. It is ideal for teams that do not require full control over their data and are willing to pay for a scalable and performant solution. NocoDB, on the other hand, is perfect for teams that value data ownership, customization, and scalability. It is particularly suitable for larger teams or organizations with the technical expertise to self-host and manage their database.

## Migration Path
1. Export data from Airtable in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up a NocoDB instance on a self-hosted server.
3. Use the NocoDB import tool to migrate data from the exported Airtable files.

## Our Take
NocoDB is not yet production-ready for most users due to its limited documentation and community support. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that NocoDB requires a significant amount of technical expertise to set up and manage. However, for teams that value data ownership and customization, NocoDB is a clear winner, and we recommend switching from Airtable to NocoDB for teams with the necessary technical expertise and a strong need for self-hosting.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that do not require collaborative features and want full control over their data.
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) that are technically proficient and want to reduce costs.
* Large teams (more than 50 users) that require high scalability and customization.
* Teams that do not need a large ecosystem of integrations and plugins.
* Teams that prioritize data ownership and are willing to manage their own servers.

## FAQ
### Can I use NocoDB for free?
Yes, NocoDB is free and self-hosted, allowing for full control over data ownership and costs.
### Is NocoDB suitable for small teams?
Yes, NocoDB can be suitable for small teams that are technically proficient and want full control over their data.
### Can I migrate my data from Airtable to NocoDB?
Yes, you can export your data from Airtable in CSV or JSON format and import it into NocoDB using the import tool.
### Is NocoDB production-ready?
No, NocoDB is not yet production-ready for most users due to its limited documentation and community support.
### Can I use NocoDB with a large team?
Yes, NocoDB is highly scalable and can be used with large teams, but it requires significant technical expertise to set up and manage.
